A .build file from a trusted build creator

A .build file is a DATA file that stores a build's passive tree, ascendancy, skills, gear notes, and planner stages. It is not an executable program, and the Build Planner does not calculate real DPS - it only guides your in-game choices.

A .build file is a JSON data file the Build Planner reads to draw a guided overlay inside the game. It stores the build author, a description, ascendancy, passive allocations, recommended skills and support gems, and inventory gear notes.
A .build file is plain data, not a program, so it cannot execute code on its own. That said, only download .build files from trusted creators and communities you recognise.

A Belt provides a limited number of Charm sockets; the exact count depends on the Belt. Check the in-game Belt tooltip for your socket total.

A Breach is an end-game map encounter marked by Clasped Hands. Entering it opens a breach that spills monsters; killing them before the breach closes banks Splinters.

A Charm is a trinket carried in a Belt that watches for a specific condition and fires automatically when that condition occurs. An Immunity Charm triggers and fully prevents the linked ailment; a Resistance Charm instead grants a temporary resistance boost when its trigger hits.

A Charm is carried in a Belt and auto-triggers when its linked condition occurs (for example becoming Frozen). It consumes Charges, which refill at Wells or by killing monsters. Immunity Charms fully prevent the linked ailment instead of just reducing it.
A Curse that feels strong on packs can look weak on a boss because bosses commonly have reduced Curse Effect. The debuff is still applied, just weaker.
A Delirium Mirror appears in a map. Walking into it spreads fog across the area; monsters inside the fog are buffed and drop better loot.
A Delirium Mirror is the entry point. Touching it wakes the fog, which then creeps outward from the mirror.
A Dexterity build maximising avoidance, backed by Block or Energy Shield.

A Grand Expedition is the larger, endgame Expedition encounter. In 0.5.4 it rolls 1-2 Expedition Map Modifiers onto the area, and three new modifiers were added: increased Runic Monster Markers, Runic Monsters are Duplicated, and the area contains additional Remnants.
A Hit is a single, discrete instance of damage dealt at a moment in time. Most Attacks and Spells deal damage as Hits, and Hits can crit, leech, and trigger on-hit effects.

An Omen is a currency that changes how your NEXT crafting action behaves. Right-click it in your inventory to make it active, then use the matching orb - the Omen modifies that single action and is consumed.

An Omen is consumed the moment the modified action happens. If you use the matching currency, the Omen applies its effect to that single use and is spent. If you never use the matching currency, the Omen stays armed until you do (or until you log out, depending on the Omen).

Armour is NOT a fixed percentage reduction. Its effectiveness scales with the size of the hit: it mitigates a larger share of many small hits and a smaller share of one enormous hit. This is why a build that feels safe against trash can suddenly die to a single boss slam.
Armour is one of the three classic defence layers. It reduces the physical damage portion of hits that actually land on you.

Because Exposure and Curses lower the enemy's actual resistance, Damage over Time benefits from them. Penetration is applied per hit, so a standalone Damage over Time instance that is not itself a hit generally does not receive Penetration. The exact Damage over Time interaction is version-sensitive — see the worked examples and treat precise values as pending PC verification.
Because Grand Expeditions carry modifiers, they are strictly more dangerous than a normal Remnant - run them only when your build already clears empowered packs comfortably.
Because More multipliers multiply, a few of them often beat stacking many Increased bonuses of the same category.
Because Penetration is the final step and local to the attacker, it does not alter the enemy's persistent resistance and does not interfere with inversion the way Exposure and Curses do.

Because evasion is probabilistic, it can fail several times in a row. A hit that does get through lands at full damage: evasion does not reduce the damage of hits that connect. This is the classic 'evasion still gets hit' complaint.
Because mapping floods charges from kills and status effects, players assume bosses do too. Bosses resist those triggers, so plan separate generation.

Because of this, avoid claiming a boss is fully immune or fully controllable unless a current source confirms it. Treat boss ailment application as possible-but-difficult, and verify specific cases against the live client rather than assuming.

Because of this, two items can have the same Required Level but very different Item Levels, and therefore very different modifier potential. The level of the area or monster that dropped the item determines its Item Level, not your character level.
Because the window is short on bosses, commit your burst immediately rather than spreading it out.

Critical Damage
Critical Damage Bonus

Critical Damage Bonus is the extra damage a critical hit deals beyond the normal hit. In Path of Exile 2 the stat is named Critical Damage Bonus (it is the successor to the old 'Critical Strike Multiplier' terminology from earlier titles). The base value is a flat bonus on top of the hit; exact coefficients are version-sensitive and noted as pending PC verification.

Critical Damage Bonus is the extra damage applied when a hit crits. It is expressed as a bonus (for example a flat +X% on top of the normal hit) rather than as a single 'multiplier' number. All sources of Critical Damage Bonus add together.
Critical Damage Bonus: extra damage on a crit, all sources add together.

Critical Hit Chance is the probability that a given Hit becomes a critical hit. It starts from a base value (set by the weapon for attacks, or by the skill for spells), can receive flat additions, and is then raised by all your Increased Critical Hit Chance modifiers added together.
Critical Hit Chance, Critical Damage Bonus, and the Crit Transition in Path of Exile 2
Critical hit

Critical hits are one of the most misread systems in Path of Exile 2 because several distinct numbers share similar names. Getting the vocabulary right is the first step to building around crit correctly.

Critically, the hit must land first. For attacks, the Accuracy versus Evasion roll happens before the crit roll: if the attack is evaded, it never becomes a crit. A crit roll can therefore be 'wasted' on a hit that misses. Lucky and Unlucky modifiers, where they apply, affect how the crit roll is performed; describe their behavior from the current in-game tooltip.

Four concepts govern every ailment. Buildup is the meter that fills as you deal ailment damage; once buildup reaches the target's Threshold, the ailment is applied and the meter resets. Magnitude scales how strong the effect is (for example how much Chill slows you, or how much Ignite damages). Duration is how long the applied ailment lasts.
Four different concepts get tangled together when players talk about 'tags'. They answer different questions and are mostly independent of one another.

Four ideas sit at the heart of whether your damage connects. Accuracy Rating is your offensive roll for attacks; Evasion Rating is the defensive roll enemies use to avoid being hit by attacks. Chance to Hit is the resulting percentage that decides if an individual attack lands. Distance is how far your character stands from the target, and it matters specifically for ranged attacks.

Leech recovers a portion of the damage you deal as Life, Mana, or Energy Shield. The critical rule in Path of Exile 2 is that leech only applies to the Damage Type and Hit type named by the leech modifier. The 0.5 update reworked Leech. Only one Leech instance can be active per resource at a time — if several trigger, only the one with the highest recovery rate applies and the others are ignored. There is also a damage cap: a single hit is treated as dealing at most 40,000 damage for Leech calculations, so very large hits no longer scale Leech without limit. The exact per-instance recovery rate and duration are client-version dependent; confirm precise coefficients in-game.

The 0.5.4 Patch Notes state that skills granted by Unique Items use the lowest skill-level requirement and then scale up to the maximum level as their requirements are met. The notes give Lifesprig as an example: a level-20 Mana Drain granted by the item is level 1 when equipped by a level-1 character.

The 0.5.4 flow has four stages. First, you discover or find a Tower node on your Atlas. Second, you enter and clear the Tower map. Third, clearing the Tower activates a Precursor Beacon. Fourth, you place Precursor Tablets into that Tower from the Atlas screen.

These four terms describe four different ways damage interacts with enemy resistance in Path of Exile 2. Keeping them distinct is the single most common fix for resistance confusion, because two of them (Curse and Exposure) change the enemy, while one (Penetration) changes only your hit.
They are excellent in maps, weak in long boss phases with no adds.
They are independent — raising one never raises the other.

They are separate effects with their own rules. Stun interrupts the target's current action. Daze raises Stun Buildup so the enemy is easier to Heavy Stun. Pin stops movement. Freeze stops actions. Electrocute is the lightning variant that stops both movement and action. None of them are interchangeable.
They are set-specific by design
They let one character run two real builds - for example a melee set and a ranged set, or a fire set and a lightning set - without overloading a single passive path.
